Neonates of the Atlantic stingray are born with a disc width of 13 cm [Lb = 13 cm], a size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated during gestation. Field surveys in estuarine habitats indicate that this species attains a maximum disc width of 61 cm [Li = 61 cm], a value documented from the largest individuals captured in coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico. The disc width at which the onset of sexual maturation typically occurs has been recorded at 22 cm [Lp = 22 cm], marking the transition to a reproductively viable stage. Gravid females carrying one to three pups per litter [N_R_i = one to three pups per litter] are commonly observed during spring and summer months, and reproductive data suggest that each female produces a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This modest annual fecundity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a relatively long-lived elasmobranch that invests heavily in individual offspring.

The maximum published wet weight for a wild-caught Atlantic stingray stands at 4900 grams [Wwi = 4900 grams], a figure recorded from an exceptionally large female in a Florida estuary. This asymptotic mass is substantially greater than the body weights typical of other members of the Dasyatidae family at similar disc widths, suggesting that Hypanus sabinus exhibits a robust somatic growth trajectory. Individuals collected during long-term monitoring programs have rarely exceeded 4.5 kilograms, making the 4900-gram record an outlier that likely represents an aged, well-nourished specimen near the end of its life span. The species' capacity to reach such a body mass is facilitated by its opportunistic diet, which includes polychaetes, small crustaceans, and benthic mollusks. Comparative data from related stingray species indicate that body mass at maximum disc width is influenced by both habitat productivity and the energetic demands of reproduction.

At a typical ambient temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], embryonic development in the Atlantic stingray proceeds at a rate heavily influenced by ambient temperature, and gestation under these thermal conditions requires approximately 122 days [ab = approximately 122 days] from fertilisation to parturition. This incubation period, equivalent to roughly four months, aligns well with the gestation lengths reported for other viviparous batoids of similar body size. The yolk-dependent embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves during this interval, undergoing organogenesis and achieving a fully formed disc before being born as a free-swimming pup. The consistency of this developmental window at 25.5 °C has been corroborated by both field observations of gravid females and controlled laboratory holding studies. Slight deviations from this temperature can lengthen or shorten the gestation period by several days, reflecting the thermal sensitivity of metabolic processes in early life stages.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Atlantic stingray in the wild is approximately 29 years [am = approximately 29 years] when the animals are maintained at a water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], a longevity that places Hypanus sabinus among the longer-lived members of its genus. This extended life span, documented through mark-recapture studies and validated by vertebral band counts, is characteristic of a species that experiences relatively low natural mortality once it reaches adult body size. The slow pace of ageing in this stingray is linked to its benthic lifestyle, which reduces predation risk, and to its moderate reproductive output, which does not impose severe metabolic costs. Individuals approaching senescence typically show reduced condition factors, slower growth increments, and a decline in reproductive activity. The relationship between temperature and longevity remains a subject of ongoing investigation, but the 25.5 °C thermal regime appears to maximise the trade-off between metabolic rate and somatic maintenance.

The reproductive biology of the Atlantic stingray is characterised by a relatively low maximum reproductive output, yielding an estimated 2 young per year [Ri = 2 young per year] when females are maintained under optimal thermal conditions of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This annual output, derived from a single litter of one to three pups combined with a single annual breeding event, underscores the species' k-selected life-history strategy. The peak reproductive effort is concentrated in the warmer months, when water temperatures approach 25.5 °C and prey availability is at its highest. Gravid females show a marked increase in food consumption, allocating resources toward both somatic maintenance and the developing embryos. The timing of parturition appears to be synchronised with seasonal productivity cycles, ensuring that newborn pups encounter favourable foraging conditions immediately after birth. This coordination between reproductive timing and environmental cues is a hallmark of elasmobranch life histories in temperate estuarine ecosystems.
